title: How To Handle A Student Who Habitually Calls Out https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2013/05/11/how-to-handle-a-student-who-habitually-calls-out/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Responding to reader questions, Linsin outlines a compassionate, multi-step approach for a student—often new to the class—who habitually calls out despite repeated consequences. The plan involves privately assuring the student that raising her hand guarantees she'll be heard, proving this by never responding to call-outs, making brief but non-responsive eye contact when she calls out anyway, and letting her experience quiet success without excessive praise. Only once she settles into the new habit does the teacher resume enforcing consequences for calling out. He frames chronic call-outs as often originating in a previous classroom where calling out was the only way to be heard, likening the student to 'a lion cub that doesn't get enough to eat.'
points: Chronic call-outs often stem from a new student's prior classroom, where calling out was the only way to be heard.
Step 1: privately assure the student that raising her hand guarantees she'll be called on—and that call-outs will never be answered.
Step 2: prove it by never responding to a call-out, even briefly, since answering even once reinforces the habit for her and others.
Step 3: make brief, non-responsive eye contact when she calls out as a private reminder, then call on someone else.
Step 4: let her experience quiet, un-praised success with raised hands before resuming consequences for future call-outs.
quotes: Namely, how do you deal with a student who, despite receiving consequence after consequence, continues to call out in class?
Like a lion cub that doesn’t get enough to eat, she has learned that she must assert herself or get pushed to the margins.
She also needs to know that you will never respond to her when she calls out. Hearing this plainly and clearly from you will relieve a good deal of the internal stress that is causing the habit.
Instead, make brief but pleasant eye contact with her (2-3 seconds) and then call on someone else.
When you do notice her sitting quietly with her hand raised—and you will—casually call on her like you would any other student.
Responding to students who call out is the very thing that encourages it—along with encouraging a host of other disruptive behavior.
